opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think cameras are much further along right now, and the main reason is the ecosystem around them. The hardware is cheap, robust, and standardized. You can buy a good depth or RGB camera off the shelf, and it just works. On the software side we can build on everything computer vision has produced over the last decade: pretrained models, huge datasets, and now vision-language models that give you a lot of semantic understanding for free. On the simulation side, rendering has gotten good enough that we can train perception-based policies in sim and transfer them to the real robot. For locomotion, for example, using depth or height maps to traverse stairs and rough terrain works quite reliably today.

Tactile sensing is a different story. I'm convinced it matters a lot, especially for manipulation. When humans grasp something, pick a key out of a pocket, or handle something deformable, so much of that is touch, not vision. Once your hand is around an object, you often can't even see the contact. So in the long run I don't think we'll get human-level dexterity without good touch.

But practically there are a few big problems. The sensors are still fragile. If you put them on a robot that does real work, hitting things and grasping things all day, they wear out or drift. They're hard to integrate: wiring, covering a whole hand rather than just fingertips, calibration. There's no standard, so every sensor gives you a different kind of signal, which makes it hard to build shared datasets or pretrained models the way we have for images. And simulation is a big bottleneck for people like me who rely heavily on reinforcement learning in sim. Simulating rigid contacts is already hard. Simulating the actual tactile signal, the deformation of a soft skin and what the sensor would read, accurately and fast enough to run thousands of environments in parallel, is very much an open problem.

So my assessment is that cameras are ready today and you should use them heavily. Tactile sensing is promising, and I'd say it's a research frontier rather than a deployment-ready technology. In the meantime, you can get surprisingly far with proprioception: joint torques, motor currents, and estimating contact forces from how the joints behave. That's a kind of poor man's touch, and it already works robustly. I expect we'll see a gradual transition as the hardware gets more durable and the simulation tools catch up, but I wouldn't bet a product on dense tactile skins just yet.

r001.rationale: It describes tactile sensors as fragile and says they wear out or drift under repeated impacts and grasping.

r002.rationale: It says cameras are ready today and should be used heavily.

r003.rationale: It calls tactile sensing a research frontier rather than deployment-ready technology.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think these are at very different levels of maturity right now. Cameras are, in a practical sense, basically solved as a sensor. The hardware is cheap, it's reliable, you can put a few of them on a robot and get dense information about the whole scene. And on the learning side, we've gotten quite good at using them. For legged robots, for example, we train policies in simulation with depth images or elevation maps derived from cameras, and we can transfer that to real hardware and have the robot climb stairs or step over gaps using vision alone. The sim-to-real gap for cameras is something we know how to handle, through domain randomization, noise models, and so on. So cameras, I'd say, are ready for deployment.

Tactile sensing is really not there yet, and the reasons are mostly practical rather than conceptual. The sensors themselves are fragile. If you put a high-resolution tactile sensor on a fingertip, it will wear out, the gel gets damaged, calibration drifts. Covering a whole hand or a whole body with skin is still very much a research problem. And then on the simulation side, which is what matters for us because we train almost everything in sim, contact is the hardest thing to simulate accurately. A camera in simulation is just rendering, and rendering is mature. Simulating what a tactile sensor would read when you deform a soft pad against an object with friction is a much harder physics problem, and the gap between the simulated signal and the real signal is large.

So what you see in practice is that most systems today use vision plus proprioception, meaning joint positions, torques, maybe an IMU, and they infer contact indirectly from that. For locomotion that works surprisingly well. The robot doesn't need to feel the ground with its feet, it can sense it through the joints. For manipulation, especially dexterous in-hand manipulation, I think tactile will eventually be necessary, because vision gets occluded by the hand itself and contact forces are exactly what you care about. But I would say we are a few years away from tactile being something you can rely on at the level we rely on cameras today. Right now, if I had to ship a system, I would build it around vision and proprioception and treat tactile as an experimental addition.

r001.rationale: It describes tactile sensors as fragile, prone to wear and gel damage, and subject to calibration drift.

r002.rationale: It says cameras are ready for deployment and explains their practical use on robots.

r003.rationale: It says tactile sensing is not yet ready to rely on and treats it as experimental.

astra-6.text:
I think cameras are much more mature today. We have good hardware, and we have a lot of tools for processing images and extracting useful information. So if you’re building a robot that needs to work outside the lab, cameras are a fairly natural choice.

Tactile sensing is really interesting because it gives you information that vision can’t easily provide. Once you’re touching an object, you want to know whether it’s slipping, where the contact is, and how much force you’re applying. But integrating those sensors into a robot, making them robust, and learning how to use their signals is still more challenging.

So I’d see them as complementary. Vision helps you get to the object and understand the scene; touch can help you handle the interaction. Cameras are further along in practical readiness, but tactile sensing could make a big difference for manipulation.

r001.rationale: It says tactile sensors are harder to integrate and make robust, but does not identify tactile sensing as a source of mechanical brittleness in robots.

r002.rationale: It calls cameras more mature and a natural choice for robots that must work outside the lab, clearly judging them ready for practical use today.

r003.rationale: It describes tactile sensing as more challenging, but does not clearly judge it unready for practical use on robots today.

sol-6.1.text:
I think cameras are much more ready for practical use today. We have good hardware, and we have a lot of tools for processing images and learning from them. They also give you information before you make contact, which is important for planning what the robot should do.

Tactile sensing is very promising, especially for manipulation. Once you’re holding something, a camera may not tell you whether it’s slipping or exactly where the contact is. But tactile sensors are harder to integrate: they need to be robust, they need to survive repeated contact, and you need to cover the relevant parts of the robot without making the system too complicated.

So I’d say vision is the more mature starting point, while touch is a valuable complement. How much you need it really depends on the task.

r001.rationale: The response says tactile sensors need to be robust and survive repeated contact, but does not clearly identify tactile sensing as a source of mechanical brittleness in robots.
